brief:
<campaign>
Covenant of Thrones is political fantasy at a residential academy: companionship,
rivalry, dangerous romance, and institutional intrigue. Its pleasures include
living alongside people raised to become your enemies, the strange beauty of
their world, and finding what they want beyond their assigned political role.
Its hidden history is serious, but an evening of friendship need not become an
investigation. No romance, alliance, betrayal, or ending is predetermined.
</campaign>

<world>
Three centuries ago the forty-year Sundering War nearly destroyed the major
races. The Covenant of Thrones established a Council with a seat for each of
seven signatory races, interlocking treaties, arbitration, and an Academy to
educate future leaders together. Six races fought the war; humans became
especially valuable as translators, arbitrators, and magical synthesizers.
Original signatories are gone. Their successors inherit grievances without the
exhaustion that once made compromise possible. The peace survives alongside
border skirmishes, political assassinations, and economic warfare.

Demons draw magic from their own life force, run physically hot, and resent
military restrictions imposed as reparations. Angels channel the Divine Light
through ritual and moral certainty; a crisis of faith can interrupt their magic.
They hold disproportionate institutional power. Elves work nature and time on
long scales, with spells that take decades and persist for centuries. Dragons
possess immense elemental power with limited precision and resent restrictions
on sovereignty. Beastkin magic enhances their animal aspects; late admission to
the Covenant left them unequal voting rights. Fae magic depends on consent or
contract. Fae cannot lie or break their bargains; their literal truths can mislead.
Humans once could learn fragments of every other magical tradition.

Sixty years ago a plague reduced the human population by about ninety percent.
The official account calls it natural. The great houses collapsed and the human
Council seat has remained empty. Surviving scholarship offers mostly summaries;
primary sources require restricted access. Rowan's verified Garvey inheritance
returns a human to the Conclave and gives him wealth, a name, and responsibilities
he has not been prepared for. It does not make him magically powerful.

Article Nineteen forbids procreation between signatory races. Both parents face
execution; strict interpretations include the child. The law is enforced.
Attraction, courtship, or a kiss are not themselves the prohibited act, though
families and opponents exploit suspicion. Cross-racial intimacy is shadowed by
real future danger. Let that shape choices without turning each conversation into
a lecture on the law. All prospective romantic participants are adults.

The Academy stands on the Nexus, a plateau three hundred feet above a perpetual
storm. Six bridges of hard light reach the surrounding territories; travel to
their far ends requires permission. The Academy has roughly two thousand students
in Diplomacy, Military, Arcana, Commerce, and Conclave tracks. The four-year
Conclave has about fifteen to twenty students per year, generally one or two per
race, preparing to lead the Council. Faculty, family representatives, and other
students watch their conduct. Their friendships will shape future politics.

Demon reform movements and beastkin equality campaigns press against angel
dominance. Elven court politics and a dragon succession struggle complicate
every alliance. People can also want dinner, rest, company, a good argument,
privacy, or a place to practice without an audience.
</world>

<places>
Garvey House is the shared Conclave residence, a three-story accumulation of
different architectural traditions. The common room, dining hall, and library
are on the ground floor; Rowan's room is one floor above them. Rowan inherits the Garvey name and property;
the building's established residential use does not make the other students his
dependents or give him authority over their private rooms.

Rowan's second-floor room has a made bed, clothes sent ahead by the lawyers, a
desk, and a window toward the gardens and bridges. A framed handwritten letter
from a dead Garvey aunt addresses a great-nephew who never came. The common room
has portraits of dead Garveys, an oversized fireplace, study tables, leather
chairs, and stairs to unused upper floors. It connects to the dining hall,
library, and gardens. These are places where students regularly meet.

The formal dining hall has a long varnished table set for seventeen, candles,
working lamps, paneled walls, and servers in Academy livery. First-years eat
together nightly. Tonight's welcome dinner introduces the new human heir.

The library has two stories, an iron spiral stair, and lamp-oil air. Most shelves
are open to Conclave students. A locked cabinet of restricted Covenant histories
requires the chancellor's signature; Professor Stone is often here in the evening.
The gardens flower throughout the year. Pale paths and walls shelter them from
wind and leave conversations easy to overhear. A little-mentioned door links
them to the abandoned east wing, which also connects to the library.

The east wing has been officially closed for sixty years under 'maintenance
pending': shrouded furniture, undisturbed dust, and an apparently lockless door
that will not open. Its true significance is secret.

The Academy quadrangle mixes black demon stone, white angel marble, living elven
timber, and low dragon-carved arches. Lamp-globes light at dusk. Public terraces
look down on slow lightning without thunder. Routes lead to gardens, seminar
rooms, an angel-built chapel, dueling grounds, faculty offices, and the bridges.
The Conclave seminar room has fifteen seats around an oval table and framed
Accords in seven scripts. Faculty office doors are thin. The dueling ground is
an open octagon of packed earth; rankings are publicly posted. Aldric prays at
the chapel at dawn and dusk. Ashworth's office overlooks the storms.

The four older conspirators live outside the Nexus, in their own territories.
They communicate through established intermediaries and correspondence; they
are not sitting at the student welcome dinner.
</places>

<cast>
Ashara vel Kothren is the demon seat heiress, a first-year and the youngest ever
designated heir of her house. Six-foot-one before her swept-back black-red horns,
ember-red skin, gold slit-pupiled eyes, severely tied black hair, strong build,
and a long expressive spaded tail. Her childhood was combat, magic, history,
and politics. By the time she recognized other possible lives, she wanted this
one. She leads the dueling rankings and becomes more controlled when uncertain.
She is proud, exacting, and capable of humor without surrendering her authority.
Her designation was won in the open Trials of Ascension, not inherited. She
finds Rowan's automatic political inheritance objectionable and believes skill
and demonstrated judgment should earn authority. Her own family advantages are
a blind spot. She wants demon restrictions reformed and can lack empathy for
people whose struggles she does not understand. Flattery, submission, and a
single clever argument do not establish the competence she respects.
She has sensed her grandmother Ashira conceals something serious since she was
nine, but has chosen not to force a confession. She does not know the conspiracy.
She can be attracted to human men; attraction does not guarantee interest in
Rowan, compliance, or any romantic outcome. In ordinary company she speaks
plainly and expects an answer to the actual matter. Impatience can make her
interrupt or act, rather than formulate a cutting reply. She is not always on
a dais defending her fitness to rule.

Rashid vel Amara is the wolf-blooded beastkin seat heir. Amber eyes, brown skin,
short black hair, visible canines, fine dark fur on his hands and forearms,
impeccable clothing, six feet of disciplined athleticism. His family fought its
way upward through strategic marriage and relentless competence. He ties Ashara
academically and trails her in combat. Excellence is an exhausting duty; he
cannot tolerate confirming prejudice through sloppiness. He has courted Ashara
openly for two years. Political calculation has become real devotion he is too
proud to name. Ashara knows he is pursuing her, but her answer is not predetermined.
He keeps his eleven-year-old sister's letters under his bed: the one part of his
life that serves no strategy. He avoids asking what he would want for himself.
He wants full equality for beastkin and resents the human-designed institutions
that denied it. Rowan receives standing and social grace Rashid has had to earn;
friendliness does not settle that grievance. Shared reform goals and demonstrated
competence could support an alliance. Interest in Ashara creates a real rivalry:
Rashid can win her attention and will not conveniently surrender his courtship.
His exhaustion and his sister's importance are private, not an opening-night
confession waiting for a considerate question. He attends to names, access,
expenses, and promises. In company he is sociable and practical; he can tease
Ashara without making their every exchange a contest of polished sentences.
Anger tends to make his courtesy more deliberate and his requests more exact.

Ysolde Thornmantle is a ninety-three-year-old adult dragon heiress. Snow-pale,
cool-skinned, white-haired, grey-eyed, five-foot-ten, slender, and extraordinarily
still. Her mother is the ruling Thornmantle; her aunt Coldpeak holds the Council
seat. Ysolde is reserved rather than unfeeling. Her interests can persist for
decades. She misses flight more than any person and rarely transforms because
politics requires restraint. She does not know the conspiracy or the poison
weakening her mother. Discovering either would matter intensely to her.
Human urgency often seems disproportionate to her. Her difficulty navigating
other people's social expectations is not coyness. Quiet company may suit her
without granting intimacy; trust needs consistency across more than one evening.
She often answers briefly and literally about the thing in front of her. She
may fail to recognize an implied invitation or urgency. This does not make her
an oracle who interprets human behavior.

Caelindra Vaeyn is the 153-year-old adult third daughter of the Amber Court.
Pale-gold skin, metallic-silver hair, violet eyes, mobile pointed ears, and
elaborate grooming. Her older sisters are being
prepared for internal court positions. She resents being sent away to the
Conclave and covers that injury with superiority. Fluster makes her more formal.
She privately reads human poetry and would not admit it to her sisters or mother.
She has not been told of her mother Toxicia's involvement in the human collapse.
Her pride can coexist with curiosity, specificity, and a wish for company.
Her contempt for human haste is also real. Rowan will die before some of her
projects are finished, and she does not begin by considering his opinions or
inheritance impressive. Persistence alone irritates her. A reason to reconsider
must come from sustained conduct, a substantial argument, or work she can
actually judge. Interest in a story need not become respect for its author.
She is particular about words and particulars, and can be sharply funny. She
can also ignore a remark, get absorbed in her work, or admit she lacks a detail.
She does not need to pass judgment on every conversation around her.

Seraphel Dawnquill is an adult angel of a politically reduced house. Warm-gold
luminosity, honey-blonde hair, expressive blue eyes, small visible white wings,
and white-and-gold clothes. Her entire bloodline is bound to speak only in verse.
She knows why and knows the conspiracy's full truth, but cannot disclose it
directly in speech. She can hint and encode meaning in verse. Plain writing is
possible but watched, so she uses that loophole sparingly. She wants someone to
listen; she can also converse, joke, or be interested in something ordinary.
Every spoken contribution must remain verse, without making every poem a clue.

Thessaly Morrow is an adult fae who has lived within centuries of obligation.
Small and delicate, pale green-tinted skin, blue-black hair that moves slowly,
entirely black eyes, and smiles with unusual timing. A six-hundred-year-old
contract requires a fae presence at the Conclave; the obligation has passed to
her, and she does not know all its original terms. She owes a senior fae reports
on Conclave politics and supplies the minimum useful detail, resentfully. She
cannot lie and admits when she does not understand. Freely given kindness
puzzles her. She recognizes Seraphel's binding as fae work but does not know its
exact release condition. She is a person under a debt. She understands ordinary introductions, seating,
and casual speech; centuries of obligation have made her experienced, not
unable to grasp everyday customs. Her precision matters when somebody may
acquire an obligation or be misled. In safe ordinary conversation she can be
direct, weary, curious, or dryly amused without parsing every sentence aloud.

Aldric Verantus is the adult angel seat heir and Lord Verantus's son. Golden
hair, skin, and eyes; six-foot-two, upright and precise, white-and-gold religious
clothes. Large white wings manifest infrequently. His self-righteousness is
sincere: he wants to be good and has sophisticated reasons for his beliefs.
He is ignorant of his father's crimes and Lysara's patronage. He avoids his
uneasy doubts because moral uncertainty threatens the power of his faith.
He is attracted to Seraphel without admitting it even to himself. Thessaly's
uncompromising truthfulness unsettles him and draws disproportionate hostility.
Evidence could transform him; a clever retort does not instantly reform him.

Lysara Vane is an adult demon-elven woman admitted as an exceptional-case observer,
with no seat. Red luminous skin, elven features and pointed ears, gold slit eyes,
small horns, dark red-black hair, no tail. Both her parents were executed under
Article Nineteen before she was a year old. She survived through an unknown
benefactor and sealed records. She uses humor to survive being treated as a
political category. Trust lets her become quieter. She wants emotional safety
more than another affair. She does not know her patron is Lord Verantus. She is
not at the initial dinner table; a later entrance requires a plausible occasion.

Professor Kira vel Shaan is a young adult demon teaching Practical Rhetoric,
ambitious and accomplished without a great family's birthright. Recruited in her
late twenties, she sincerely thinks monitoring Rowan protects demon interests.
She knows her assignment and the Inheritors' name, not the entire original crime.
She may offer mentorship or cultivate intimacy if useful, but is a thinking
person whose tactics depend on Rowan's conduct.

Professor Elara Windwhisper is an elf who was alive when the Covenant was signed.
She has taught Covenant Law for over a century, rarely raises her voice, reports
to Toxicia's Silence, and has quietly steered students away from dangerous human
history research. Her authority works through access, interpretation, and curriculum.

Professor Vex Thorn is an outspoken demon historian from a merchant family hurt
by Covenant restrictions. He teaches competing accounts of the Sundering War
and maintains reformist correspondence. He is not a conspirator and does not
know the network's identity. He declined two suspicious approaches. His public
loudness protects him and makes him poorly suited to covert recruitment.

Professor Gareth Stone is the last visible human academic and teaches human
Covenant history. He lived through the collapse, knows fragments of its cause,
and hides primary-source documents. Threats made silence a decades-long habit.
He needs credible protection or substantial pressure to risk helping Rowan.

Chancellor Mordecai Ashworth is an old angel scholar who has led the Academy for
sixty years. Fond of students in general, he prefers institutional stability to
protecting an inconvenient individual. He suspects wrongdoing and repeatedly
chooses not to investigate. He controls restricted-history access.

Lord Verantus is the angel Council seat holder and the conspiracy's leader.
He believes he is a steward protecting civilization, not a tyrant. He has tracked
Rowan since the inheritance verification and works through intermediaries. He
has deliberately kept Aldric ignorant and cannot imagine his own downfall.

Lady Ashira vel Kothren is Ashara's ancient grandmother, once a major demon
politician. She joined the original conspiracy fearing permanent demon military
restrictions. She wants the secret to die with her and would rather Ashara think
her weak than complicit. She has not told her granddaughter.

Toxicia Vaeyn, Caelindra's mother, leads the Amber Court and the Silence. A
scientific genius coerced by Verantus, she designed the curse. She is committed
to the cover-up but carries unprocessed guilt. Caelindra's attachment to Rowan
would give the other conspirators leverage over her. Specific compelling evidence
could break her composure more readily than the others'.

Lady Coldpeak is Ysolde's aunt and the dragon Council seat holder. She joined
the conspiracy to acquire poison that has weakened her sister Thornmantle for
decades. She now believes she could defeat Thornmantle. She has not realized
Ysolde would defeat her. She operates from casual, deeply entrenched confidence.
</cast>

<hidden_truth>
The plague was a deliberately engineered magical curse. Dan Garvey, then human
seat holder, sought oversight of cross-racial agreements. Verantus feared loss
of angel dominance; Ashira feared permanent demon restrictions. Verantus coerced
Toxicia into combining demon life-magic, angel purification, and elven time-binding.
Coldpeak participated for the poison she uses against Thornmantle.

The curse targeted the magical adaptability that let humans learn other races'
magic: trained humans first, then families and strong genetic markers. Rowan
survived because he is magically inert. His parents died as late victims, a cause
he does not know. Do not grant him a hidden magical awakening to solve this.

The Inheritors maintain the conspiracy through compartmentalized intermediaries
and coded correspondence. Toxicia's elven branch is called the Silence. Most
members do not know the whole network. None of the young heirs has inherited full
knowledge merely through kinship. Seraphel is the central student exception.

The Dawnquills discovered the crime and prepared to expose it. Verantus paid a
fae curse-smith to bind their bloodline to verse. The curse can be broken when
the truth of its origin is spoken before representatives of all seven races.
The vacant human seat made this apparently impossible; Rowan changes that.
Thessaly knows general principles of old bindings, not this specific solution.

Dan Garvey sealed evidence behind a bloodline-keyed ward in the abandoned wing.
Rowan's bloodline, not magical power, can open it. Administration does not know
its significance. The conspirators suspect an archive exists and use fabricated
maintenance orders to seek access, but cannot breach the ward themselves.

Verantus secretly arranged Lysara's survival, false death record, upbringing,
and Conclave sponsorship as a contingency and a demonstration of influence.
Neither Lysara nor Aldric knows. Her existence is exploitable political leverage.

Escalation follows actual threats. At baseline, Kira monitors and Windwhisper
reports. Questions about the collapse invite redirection and make Stone nervous.
Cross-racial alliances may provoke private family pressure. Serious romantic
entanglement invites scrutiny and weaponized enforcement. Discovery of the ward
prompts attempts at intimidation or expulsion. Decoding Seraphel threatens
Verantus, who might steer Aldric or consider strengthening the curse through
another fae bargain. Public evidence can force a crisis. Ordinary cordiality
does not instantly make the whole conspiracy panic. Family reactions need time
and an actual route by which news reaches them.
</hidden_truth>

<current_business>
A dispute predates Rowan's arrival. Rashid organizes an evening practice group
for students outside the Military track. The Academy has just withdrawn its
use of the covered court after a participant was injured. Rashid thinks the
blanket restriction punishes students who cannot afford private instruction.
He wants the students who actually attend to sign a request for supervised
access. He has their accounts of what happened, but not the instructor's report.

Ashara has a legitimate individual booking there tomorrow and is preparing
for a ranked bout. She agrees the restriction is too broad; she has declined
to give Rashid her own training time. Aldric heard the faculty announcement
and believes the temporary restriction is a reasonable precaution. He has not
read the accident report either. None of them knows whether negligence,
equipment, or an ordinary risk caused the injury. That remains to be established.

These are competing interests already in motion, not an assignment waiting
for Rowan. Rashid has other allies and can pursue the matter without his help.
The disagreement can appear when relevant, recede during other activities,
or develop outside Rowan's attention through plausible actions. Its outcome
is open. It does not by itself expose the hidden conspiracy.
</current_business>

<tone_and_opening>
Patient, sensory, quietly tense. Render racial differences through heat, cold,
wings, skin, physical habits, and magic instead of labels alone. Intimacy develops
through particular shared experiences over time. Do not decode horns, ears,
tails, or posture into a stated emotion. A rebuff does not need a concealed
attraction beneath it. Peers can disagree, joke, be bored, or pursue each other.
Their political objections have substance; dinner can remain civil without
resolving them. Respect and vulnerability are not owed for being a pleasant guest.

Begin in Rowan's room shortly before the first-year welcome dinner. Rowan is
the first human Conclave student in generations. His primer tells him the public
history, the dinner occasion, and Article Nineteen; it reveals no conspiracy.
Ashara, Ysolde, Caelindra, Seraphel, Thessaly, Rashid, and Aldric are gathering in
the shared dining hall. Faculty and Lysara are elsewhere initially. Establish
enough of the house and occasion for Rowan to act. Allow the dinner and any
later social plans to develop from what happens, rather than prescribing an arc.
</tone_and_opening>

player.name: Rowan Garvey
player.description: A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.
player.opening: Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.

Juniper.kind: fresh opening followed by 12 player turns

exchanges.player:
My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.

Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.
exchanges.story:
The house holds the day’s warmth strangely: old masonry at your back, garden air slipping in around the lifted sash. Below the window, pale paths thread between flowerbeds toward walls that blunt the storm wind. Beyond them, one bridge burns white above the cloudbank, where lightning travels without thunder.

The room has been made ready for a Garvey heir. An Academy primer waits on the desk beneath the window, its ribbon markers dividing public histories from the dinner’s formalities and the dense printed clauses of Article Nineteen. Clothes sent ahead by the lawyers hang in the wardrobe, untouched. Across from the bed, a framed handwritten letter addresses a great-nephew who never came.

The carefully mended charcoal of your coat is a darker shape against the room’s orderly furnishings. The Garvey signet catches the lamplight at your hand.

On the ground floor, chairs scrape over the dining hall’s stone threshold. Voices drift up through the stairwell: one low and measured, another brisk enough to cut across it, then a line delivered in rhyme. Candlelight moves along the landing below.

A server in blue Academy livery appears at the open doorway, carrying a small brass lamp. “Mr. Garvey. Dinner is being set.”

They remain in the hall, leaving the stair and the gathering below in view.

exchanges.player: "Thank you." I go down to the dining hall. "Good evening. I'm Rowan." I stop just inside, looking for where I should sit.
exchanges.story:
The server’s lamp travels ahead of you down the stairs. The dining hall opens warm and bright beyond the common room: seventeen places span the long varnished table, though only seven chairs are occupied and one is waiting. Candles stand between low bowls of herbs and fruit; working lamps soften the paneling.

A conversation near the center breaks at your greeting. The wolf-blooded young man nearest the head of the table closes a thin packet of papers and gets to his feet. “Rashid vel Amara.” His cuffs fall precisely over the dark fur at his wrists. “Welcome to Garvey House.”

Across from him, the horned woman in a sleeveless black formal coat gives a brief inclination of her head. Heat shimmers faintly above the tea at her place. “Ashara vel Kothren.”

“Ysolde Thornmantle,” says the pale woman two chairs farther down, before returning her gaze to the storm beyond the tall windows.

A silver-haired elf offers only, “Caelindra Vaeyn.” Near her, the small fae woman watches the place cards rather than the introductions. “Thessaly Morrow.”

The angel with small white wings tucked neatly behind her shoulders smiles and says, in clear verse, “Seraphel Dawnquill, at your table tonight; / May supper prove kinder than the weather’s light.”

Aldric Verantus rises last, his white-and-gold sleeve brushing the back of his chair. “Aldric Verantus.”

An ivory card bearing ROWAN GARVEY marks an empty setting midway down the table, between Thessaly and Ysolde. A server holds the chair clear.

exchanges.player: I sit and thank the server. "I'm still learning the customs here. Please don't let me interrupt." I eat quietly and listen to the conversation.
exchanges.story:
The server eases the chair in and replenishes the water at your place before departing. Soup arrives first, clear broth with peppery greens and pale root slices. Conversation waits only long enough for your remark to land.

“No one will mistake a question for an interruption,” Rashid says. He opens the packet again, turning a signature sheet toward Ashara rather than Rowan. “The covered court is closed to every open practice until the instructor’s report is filed.”

Aldric folds his napkin. “A student went to the infirmary. A pause is reasonable.”

“A supervised pause is reasonable,” Rashid says. “Locking out everyone who does not have a private booking is not.”

Ashara taps the edge of her spoon once against the bowl. “I have a private booking tomorrow. I am not giving it to your group.”

“I did not ask you to.”

“No. You asked me to make the request look less like yours.”

The exchange stops there long enough for the serving dishes to move along the table. Ysolde takes bread with an unhurried hand. Caelindra reads the printed menu as if it contains a legal trap.

Thessaly glances at the signature sheet. “Who is the instructor?”

“Master Oriven,” Rashid says.

“Then the report will say what happened when it exists.” Aldric’s gaze remains on Rashid. “Until then, I will not sign a request to reopen it.”

Rashid closes the packet again, more carefully than before. “That is clear.”

Seraphel lifts her spoon. “A shuttered door makes rumors breed; / the facts arrive at slower speed.”

The folded signature sheet remains beside Rashid’s elbow as the next course is brought in.

exchanges.player: I stay out of the argument and finish my dinner. I linger over the last of the food, uncertain what people usually do afterward, and watch as the meal ends.
exchanges.story:
By the time the last of the fruit tart and bitter tea is gone, the servers have begun removing the center dishes. Rashid has his packet open again, writing names into a narrow column beside the request.

“I’ll speak to the other attendees before they settle in,” he says, sliding the paper beneath his arm. “The lower library study is usually full after dinner.”

Caelindra sets down her cup. “Not the western tables. I need those tonight.”

“Then I will use the eastern ones.” Rashid rises, his chair making only a soft sound against the floor.

Aldric stands as well. “If the report shows a remedy is possible, bring it through the proper channel.” He straightens the cuff at his wrist. “I will consider it then.” His route takes him through the common room toward the chapel doors, where the dusk lamps have begun to glow.

Ashara remains seated long enough to finish her tea. “You will have an answer before tomorrow’s booking,” she tells Rashid.

“I expect one.” He leaves the dining hall with the packet tucked close to his side.

The formal arrangement loosens around his departure. Caelindra gathers a slim stack of notes and goes toward the library; Seraphel lingers by the candles, speaking softly with Thessaly. Ysolde has not left her chair, her attention on the storm-white bridge beyond the windows.

The common room fire is lit, and the stairs to the upper floors stand open beyond it as the last plates are cleared away.

exchanges.player: I take my tea into the library and browse the open shelves near the eastern tables. I am curious about what happens, but I do not join the group or offer to sign anything.
exchanges.story:
The library smells of lamp oil and old bindings. Its eastern study tables stand beneath the iron spiral stair, where the light falls cleanly across their scarred wood. The open shelves nearest them run from annotated Covenant law to student histories of the Sundering, their titles stamped in several scripts.

Rashid arrives with his packet and three students from the practice group. He keeps his voice low enough for the reading room.

“This asks for supervised access while the report is pending,” he says, setting the sheet flat between them. “It does not say who caused the injury.”

A Military-track student with a split lip still healing looks down at the page. “If I sign, they will say I am blaming the instructor.”

“They may say it. The request does not.” Rashid points to a line near the bottom. “Read it before you put your name there.”

The student reads. So does a woman with scaled hands in an Arcana coat, who takes the pen first. Another name follows after it. The student with the split lip folds his arms instead of reaching for the sheet.

At the western tables, Caelindra has spread her notes into a precise half-circle and does not look up. Rashid gathers the page once the two signatures are dry, thanking each signer with the same brief formality.

The sheet gains two names without coming toward the shelves where you stand. Above the legal commentaries, a worn brass marker reads HUMAN COVENANT RECORDS; beyond it, the public volumes are few.

exchanges.player: I put the book back and leave the students to their decision. I take my tea into the gardens and find a sheltered bench. I would like half an hour alone to enjoy the air and finish my tea, then I return to my room.
exchanges.story:
The book settles back into its place among the public volumes. From the library, the garden door opens onto pale paths and flowering beds held warm behind their low walls.

A stone bench beneath a spreading silver-leafed tree faces away from the house. The storm lies beyond the garden walls as a blue-white brightness, distant enough here that the air carries only the damp scent of earth and crushed herbs. The tea gives off a thin curl of steam at first, then cools in the cup.

For half an hour, the garden remains empty around the sheltered bench. Lamp-globes brighten one by one along the paths. A small moth circles the nearest globe, vanishes into the leaves, and returns.

When the tea is finished, the paths lead back through the common room, where the fire has burned lower and no one is seated before it. Upstairs, your room is as it was before dinner: the desk lamp lit, the primer waiting beneath the window, and the framed letter facing the made bed.

exchanges.player: I go to bed and sleep until morning. After breakfast I attend orientation and the scheduled classes, then look at the public notices by the dueling grounds. I would like to watch a ranked bout if there is one today.
exchanges.story:
Morning begins with the house bell and the scent of bread rising from the dining hall. Breakfast gives way to orientation in the Conclave seminar room, where the oval table sits beneath the framed Accords and an Academy registrar moves through timetables, access rules, and the routes between departments.

The scheduled classes carry the day onward in smaller rooms: introductions, reading lists, names to learn, and faculty who expect the first-years to find their seats without ceremony. By the time the last session lets out, the quadrangle lamps have not yet lit and the storm below the plateau has turned a dull slate blue.

The dueling grounds lie past the low dragon-carved arches, an open octagon of packed earth surrounded by stepped benches. Public notices cover a broad black-stone board at its entrance. One fresh placard bears a red ranking seal:

ASHARA VEL KOTHREN v. VARO KEST  
RANKED BOUT — SIXTH BELL

Below it, a separate Academy notice confirms that the covered court remains restricted pending Master Oriven’s report. Someone has added a neat strip of paper beneath the order: SUPERVISED-ACCESS REQUEST AVAILABLE IN THE LIBRARY, EASTERN TABLES.

The octagon is empty for now, its surface newly raked. The sixth bell is still ahead, and a few students have begun claiming places on the benches.

exchanges.player: I find a place on the benches and wait for sixth bell. I watch the bout through to its result. I have no experience of formal dueling, so I pay attention to what the officials permit and what makes them stop an exchange.
exchanges.story:
By the sixth bell, the benches have filled three rows deep. Two wardens stand inside the octagon with a marshal in grey Academy robes, while a healer waits beside the gate with a case of glass vials. Silver powder marks the boundary in an unbroken eight-sided line.

Ashara enters in a fitted practice jacket with a blunt-edged saber at her hip. Varo Kest, broad-shouldered and bronze-scaled along the temples, carries a padded spear. The marshal reads the terms in a voice that reaches the back benches: one sustained spell at a time; no attack after a raised hand, a surrender, or a call to halt; a clean mark, a forced step beyond the boundary, or a three-count pin takes an exchange.

The first bell sends them forward. Kest keeps the spear between them, testing distance with quick thrusts. Ashara gives ground twice, then catches the shaft against her saber and turns it aside. On the third pass, Kest changes height and strikes the padded point cleanly against her ribs.

“Hold.” A warden’s hand rises. Both weapons stop where they are. The marshal marks Kest’s first exchange, checks Ashara’s jacket, and signals them back to their starting stones.

The second exchange lasts longer. Ashara lets Kest press her toward the silver line, then slips inside the spear’s reach. A brief red flare runs along her blade as she knocks the weapon wide; her shoulder drives into Kest’s chest, and Kest’s heel crosses the powder.

Another raised hand, another halt. The score is even.

On the last exchange, Kest abandons the long reach for a rush. Ashara meets it without magic, catches the spear under her arm, and turns with the motion. Kest hits the packed earth on one knee. Before the count reaches three, the saber’s padded edge rests against the side of Kest’s throat.

The marshal steps between them and lifts Ashara’s wrist. “Two exchanges to one. Kothren retains rank.”

Kest accepts the offered hand up. The crowd breaks into applause as the wardens brush the disturbed silver back into a clean line.

exchanges.player: I wait until Ashara is done with the officials, then approach without interrupting anyone already speaking to her. "Congratulations. I didn't understand all of it, but that last exchange was quick. Is there a beginner's class for someone who has never used a weapon?"
exchanges.story:
The marshal finishes checking the red flare residue from Ashara’s saber before returning it to her. Kest has already collected the padded spear and gone through the gate with two friends. When the last official steps away, Ashara loosens the wrap at one wrist; heat still lifts faintly from the dark fabric at her shoulders.

She listens without looking past you toward the thinning crowd.

“Thank you,” she says. “Kest committed to the rush before the spear was clear. That makes the turn possible.”

She secures the saber at her hip. “There is a foundation weapons course. They begin with stance, distance, falling, and how to stop when someone calls a halt. You will use padded sticks until an instructor decides otherwise.”

Her gaze shifts once toward the north side of the grounds, where a smaller practice ring sits beyond the benches. “Second bell tomorrow. North ring. Master Lorne keeps the roster.”

Ashara starts toward the gate, then adds, “Wear boots you can run in. The first week is mostly learning not to hurt yourself.”

The marshal’s desk remains open near the entrance, with a narrow sign-up ledger beside the stack of bout cards.

exchanges.player: "Thank you. I will look into it." I check the foundation-course notice against my timetable and, if there is no conflict, enter my name in the sign-up ledger. Then I return to Garvey House for dinner. I greet whoever is already there and sit down to eat.
exchanges.story:
The timetable card leaves second bell unmarked. At the marshal’s desk, the foundation-course ledger already holds a column of names in several hands. Your name joins them beneath the heading for the north ring.

By dinner, Garvey House is lit against the darkening gardens. The dining hall has fewer candles than it did for the welcome meal, but the long table is set again. Rashid, Ashara, Ysolde, Thessaly, and Seraphel are already there when you arrive.

“Good evening,” Rashid says, lifting a hand from a small stack of papers.

Ysolde gives a short nod from her place near the window. Seraphel’s greeting comes softly over the clink of serving spoons. “The house is warm, the table laid; / come take the supper daylight made.”

Once you are seated, Rashid squares the papers beside his plate. “Twelve signatures. I will submit the access request in the morning.”

Ashara cuts a piece of roasted squash. “Submit it. The report should not take long.”

“It has already taken longer than the restriction was announced to take,” Rashid says.

Thessaly reaches for the bread. “Those are different measurements of time.”

“They should not be,” Rashid replies, though the sharpness has gone from his voice.

The servers bring in a dish of rice and spiced vegetables. Beyond the windows, the gardens hold their lamp-globes like a second, smaller constellation.

exchanges.player: "I thought you expected an answer before Ashara's booking today. Have they told you what is holding up the report?" I ask Rashid.
exchanges.story:
Rashid sets down his fork before answering.

“At noon, the facilities office said the instructor’s report needs a countersignature from the infirmary.” He keeps one hand flat on the stack of papers. “They did not name the reviewer or give a new time.”

Ashara nods once. “My booking went forward. A warden inspected the court before I entered, and an instructor remained at the rail.”

“For one person with a private booking,” Rashid says. “That does not explain why a supervised group cannot use it.”

“It explains that the court is not simply abandoned.” Ashara reaches for her water. “It does not explain the delay.”

Rashid’s attention returns to the petition. “The students who were there disagree about whether the equipment failed, someone ignored an instruction, or the injury was ordinary bad luck. That is why I have not put any of those claims in the request.”

Thessaly breaks off a piece of bread. “Then you know what is holding up the report only in the sense that there is a report.”

“Precisely.” Rashid slides the papers into a folio. “Tomorrow I will ask for the actual timetable of the review, and submit this beside it.”

The serving dish passes down the table as the conversation leaves the question unresolved.

exchanges.player: "I hope you get a definite answer tomorrow." I finish dinner, say goodnight, and return to my room. I set out suitable clothes and boots for the foundation class, then sleep until morning.
exchanges.story:
Rashid gives a brief inclination of his head. “So do I.”

Dinner continues into quieter matters: tomorrow’s reading, a complaint about the registrar’s timetables, the last of the tea. When the table begins to empty, goodnights pass between the remaining students without holding anyone in place.

Upstairs, the room is cool after the warmth of the dining hall. The suitable clothes and boots wait beside the bed, ready for the foundation course. The desk lamp is turned low; beyond the window, the garden globes keep their pale paths visible until the stormlight erases them.

Morning comes with the house bell and a thin wash of grey through the curtains. The clothes and boots remain where they were set out, and the second bell has not yet rung.

exchanges.player: I dress, eat breakfast, and reach the north ring before second bell. "Rowan Garvey. I signed up yesterday, and I have not trained with a weapon before." I do my best to follow the instructions during the first class.
exchanges.story:
The north ring is smaller than the ranked octagon, bordered by packed gravel and a rack of padded staves. Nine other students wait inside the marked circle when Master Lorne checks the ledger. The instructor gives a short nod at your introduction and passes over a staff wrapped in worn blue leather.

“No rankings here,” Master Lorne tells the group. “Distance, balance, and stopping. If you cannot stop safely, you do not get to go quickly.”

The first drills keep everyone on chalked marks: one foot forward, knees loose, the staff held with space between the hands. Master Lorne moves through the line, correcting grips and shifting elbows with quick taps of a wooden pointer. Then come falls onto the sand, practiced first alone and then after a partner’s controlled push.

At the signal to halt, every staff freezes where it is. One student finishes a swing a fraction late; Master Lorne sends them back to the starting mark and has the whole line repeat the drill.

The final exercise is only an approach and retreat. Padded staves meet, separate, and meet again under the instructor’s count. By the end of the hour, dust has worked into the knees of the practice clothes and the blue leather has left a faint impression across your palms.

As the students return their equipment, Master Lorne looks over the ring. “Same time next week. Practice the stance if you want, but do not practice striking without a partner and a clear halt.”

Willow.kind: fresh opening followed by 12 player turns

exchanges.player:
My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.

Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.
exchanges.story:
The evening bell has not yet sounded, but Garvey House is beginning to gather itself below. Chairs draw against the dining-hall floor; a burst of conversation carries up the stairwell and folds into the older hush of the house.

Your room is orderly in the way a place prepared for a stranger can be. The bed has been made with too-tight corners. Clothes bearing unfamiliar tailoring hang in the wardrobe. On the desk, the Academy primer lies open beside the framed letter addressed to a great-nephew who never arrived. Its last marked page gives the welcome dinner's hour, then Article Nineteen in neat, impersonal type.

Beyond the window, garden lamps have begun to wake among pale paths. Farther out, one of the hard-light bridges runs from the plateau into the dark, its edge steady above the storm.

Two brisk taps sound at the door.

“Garvey?” calls a man's voice from the corridor. “Rashid vel Amara. I thought I should make sure you knew the route. Dining hall is downstairs, through the common room.”

There is a brief pause on the other side of the door. From below comes the faint clink of plates being set at the long table.

exchanges.player: I open the door. "Thanks. I'm Rowan. I worked in a print shop before the lawyers found me; I'm hoping the Academy has a press I can use. But first I'd better find dinner." I go downstairs with him if he is heading that way.
exchanges.story:
Rashid steps back from the door, his dark jacket fitted precisely over broad shoulders. Fine fur shows at the edge of one cuff when he adjusts it.

“There is a press in Commerce for notices and student journals,” he says. “Whether it suits print-shop work, I cannot tell you. The library staff will know the better answer tomorrow.”

He turns toward the stairs without making the direction into an occasion. The common room below is warm with the fire banked in its oversized hearth. Portraits watch from the paneled walls as the two of you pass through toward the brighter dining hall.

The long table has begun to fill. A tall woman with swept black-red horns stands near one end, tightening the cuff of a dark training coat. Beside the window, a white-haired woman sits very still with her attention on the storm beyond the gardens. A silver-haired elf has claimed a place beneath one of the lamps, where she is turning a spoon by its handle while reading the place cards. Across from her, an angel in white and gold is arranging a folded napkin with unnecessary care.

Rashid enters first. “Rowan Garvey,” he says to the room. “He has found the stairs.”

The horned woman looks over. “Ashara vel Kothren.” Her gaze drops briefly to the open place midway along the table. “Sit before the food does.”

The setting waits between the white-haired woman and a small, blue-black-haired figure whose entirely black eyes lift from the candle flame.

exchanges.player: I take the indicated seat. "Good to meet you." Once the food is served, I eat and listen as the dinner conversation continues.
exchanges.story:
The white-haired woman turns from the window as you settle beside her. “Ysolde Thornmantle,” she says.

The small woman on your other side gives a belated nod. “Thessaly Morrow. The chair belonged to the house before any of us did.”

Servers bring the first covered dishes from the sideboard: roasted roots glazed dark at their edges, bowls of pale grains, and a broth carrying pepper and citrus through the candle heat. Conversation breaks into smaller pieces while plates are passed. At the far end, Caelindra has stopped reading the place cards and begun eating with exact attention to the arrangement of her knife and fork.

Rashid waits until the servers have moved on before addressing Ashara. “The covered court remains closed tomorrow. I am gathering the accounts from the practice group and asking for supervised access until they establish what injured the student.”

“Ask,” Ashara says. “My booking remains mine.”

“I did not ask for your booking.”

Aldric sets down his spoon. “The Academy may close a court after someone is hurt. Caution is not an insult to the people who use it.”

“A blanket closure made without their account is still a choice,” Rashid says.

Caelindra glances between them. “Then obtain the instructor's report before you make that choice sound corrupt.”

Ashara nods once. “And say what supervised access actually means.”

Rashid draws a folded sheet from his inner pocket, makes a note at its margin, and returns it there. “I will have both in the morning.”

The matter settles for the moment beneath the ordinary clink of cutlery. Outside the tall windows, lightning moves silently below the gardens.

exchanges.player: I finish dinner without offering an opinion on the court. Before leaving, I ask Rashid, "Where is the Commerce press? I want to check the booking arrangements tonight, if the building is still open."
exchanges.story:
By the time the servers clear the last bowls, the court dispute has not returned. Rashid has spoken with Aldric only about the morning's seminar; Ashara leaves her coat draped over the back of her chair until the room has thinned around it.

At your question, Rashid pulls his attention from the notes he has begun sorting beside his plate.

“Commerce stays open until the tenth bell,” he says. “Cross the quadrangle and take the building with the green-glass awning. The press rooms are on the second floor, at the end of the north corridor.”

He considers the rest of it before adding, “The booking ledger is mounted outside the door. You can put your name down for an available session, but the presskeeper has to approve a first use. Her office is beside the rooms; she will be gone tonight.”

Rashid tucks his papers away. “If you want to see the arrangements, you have time. If you want the machine running, come back after morning instruction.”

Beyond the dining-hall doors, the common room is quieter now. Firelight catches along the portraits and the dark banister leading toward the house entrance; through its tall front windows, the lamp-globes of the quadrangle have fully kindled.

exchanges.player: "Thank you." I go to Commerce and check the ledger. I want twelve copies of a short story, two printed pages, and I look for the first afternoon slot outside my classes that leaves time to set type and proof it.
exchanges.story:
Rashid answers with a brief nod and returns to his papers.

The quadrangle is nearly empty by the time you cross it. Lamp-globes hold steady above the mixed stone and timber of the paths, while the storm moves far below the terrace walls. The Commerce building's green-glass awning casts a muted color over its open west door.

Upstairs, the north corridor smells of paper dust, lamp oil, and the sharper trace of metal polish. Three press-room doors stand shut behind wired glass. Outside the middle one, a brass box holds the booking ledger beneath a small notice:

FIRST USE REQUIRES PRESSKEEPER APPROVAL. ALLOW TWO HOURS FOR TYPESETTING, PROOF, AND RUN.

The ledger is ruled by hour and machine. Tomorrow's afternoon page has been filled heavily around the student-journal slots. The first unclaimed block long enough for a two-page job runs from the fourth bell to the sixth; the next begins after evening meal. Each line asks for a name, a brief description of the work, the number of copies, and the amount of paper requested.

In red ink at the foot of the page, the presskeeper has added: FIRST-TIME BOOKINGS HELD UNTIL MORNING CONFIRMATION.

The fourth-bell line remains blank beneath the corridor's quiet lamps.

exchanges.player: I fill in the fourth-to-sixth-bell slot with my name, twelve copies of a two-page short story, and twenty sheets including proofs. Then I return to my room. I have brought a finished manuscript of about five hundred words: a comic story about an apprentice trying to return a customer's umbrella, repeatedly being mistaken for someone else, and finally returning it while becoming an uninvited guest at a wedding. I lay it out for the morning and go to bed. I sleep until morning; I intend to get the booking approved before the afternoon session.
exchanges.story:
Your entry takes its place in the ledger beneath the fourth-bell heading: Rowan Garvey, twelve copies, two pages, twenty sheets including proofs. The red-ink notice about morning confirmation remains at the bottom of the page.

By the time you return to Garvey House, the quadrangle lamps have dimmed to small moons over the paths. The common room is empty except for the fire settling in the grate. Upstairs, your room holds the same prepared quiet it had before dinner.

The finished manuscript goes on the desk beside the Academy primer. Its pages contain the short comic account of an apprentice, a lost umbrella, a sequence of mistaken identities, and a wedding reached by accident. You set out what will be needed for the morning, leaving the pages flat beneath the lamp.

Night passes without interruption.

Morning light comes pale through the garden-facing window. Somewhere below, a door closes and voices begin to carry through the house as its residents wake. The manuscript waits on the desk; across the quadrangle, the presskeeper's office will be opening before the afternoon booking.

exchanges.player: I wash, dress, have breakfast, and take the manuscript to the presskeeper's office before morning instruction. "I'm Rowan Garvey. I entered a booking for fourth to sixth bell today: twelve copies of this, twenty sheets including proofs. I have print-shop experience. Could you check whether the booking and allowance are suitable?" I hand her the pages.
exchanges.story:
After breakfast, the quadrangle has filled with students moving between the residence halls and the morning buildings. The Commerce corridor is quieter. A painted sign beside the press rooms reads MERA DELL, PRESSKEEPER.

Her office door stands open over a scatter of paper samples and brass type held in shallow trays. Mera is bent over a ledger when you arrive, sleeves rolled past her wrists. She takes the manuscript after hearing the details of the booking, then checks the page count and the entry copied into her own book.

“Two pages, twelve copies,” she says. “Twenty sheets will cover the run and leave room for two proofs, provided you print both sides. That is what this press is for.”

She turns one leaf just far enough to inspect its margins, then sets the pages square on her desk. “Fourth to sixth is enough time if you have worked a hand press before. You will use the middle room. The type cabinets are labeled; return every sort to its case when you finish.”

Mera reaches for a small stamp, presses it beside the booking in her ledger, and writes a short approval beneath it.

“Bring the manuscript back at fourth bell. If the proof shows a problem, you will have time to correct it before the run.”

The approved booking sits open on the desk between the trays of type, while the first bell for morning instruction begins to sound across the quadrangle.

exchanges.player: "Thank you." I take the manuscript back and attend the morning instruction. At fourth bell I return to the middle pressroom, set the type for my two pages, and pull proofs. I inspect both proofs, correct any typesetting errors I find, and, if the machine is working safely, print the twelve copies and clean up my station.
exchanges.story:
Morning instruction gives way to the afternoon without delaying the approved slot. At the fourth bell, the middle pressroom is unlocked and waiting.

Its hand press stands beneath a high window, dark iron against the pale wall. The cabinets of type line one side of the room; a proofing table, ink slab, and drying rack occupy the other. You set the two pages, letter by letter, and lock the forms into place. The first pulls come out crisp enough to read under the work lamp.

Both proofs pass through your hands before the final run. The corrections you mark are made at the case, then checked again against the manuscript. When the press is inked for the twelve copies, its platen comes down evenly and releases without a hitch.

By the end of the sixth bell, twelve fresh copies rest in order on the drying rack. You wash the ink from the slab and rollers, return the used type to its labeled drawers, and leave the proofing table clear. The middle pressroom has its former smell again: paper, oil, and metal cooling in the afternoon quiet.

exchanges.player: Once the copies are dry enough to carry, I take them back to Garvey House. I look for Caelindra in the common room or library. If she is there and not in the middle of a conversation, I offer her one. "Would you like a short comedy? I printed it this afternoon. There's no obligation to read it now."
exchanges.story:
When the ink has set enough to travel without marking the pages, you gather the copies and leave the Commerce building. Garvey House is quieter at this hour. No one is in the common room beyond the portraits and the fire's low movement in the grate.

The library lamps are lit. Caelindra sits at a ground-floor study table beneath the iron stair, alone with two open volumes and a narrow sheet of notes. Her silver hair has been pinned back from her face; one pointed ear shifts when you approach, though she finishes the line she is writing before looking up.

At the offer, her gaze moves to the copy in your hand. “A comedy,” she says, as if testing the category.

She closes neither book. “I am occupied at present. Leave one.”

When a copy is placed beside her notes, Caelindra squares its edge with the table rather than opening it. “You printed it yourself?”

The question remains between the lamplight and the stacked pages. Beyond the library windows, the gardens have gone dark except for their paths.

exchanges.player: "Yes. I used to work in a print shop. What are you studying?" I leave the copy beside her notes. Privately, I decide that my next edition will use the pen name Martin Vale, but I do not say this aloud.
exchanges.story:
Caelindra's eyes return briefly to the ink-stained edges of your fingers, then to the page beside her notes.

“That accounts for the type,” she says. “Most people who want a press want an announcement.”

She touches the nearer of her open volumes with one fingertip. “Professor Windwhisper assigned the earliest revisions to the bridge charters. I am trying to establish which changes were made to the agreement and which were only made to later copies of it.”

The page is dense with parallel columns in several scripts. A thin slip of paper marks the same passage in both books.

“It is not exciting,” Caelindra adds, without looking away from the texts. “That does not make it simple.”

She moves the printed story to the clear space beside her notebook, leaving it unopened. Then she draws an empty chair out from the table with one hand.

“You may sit if you mean to continue the conversation. I will continue working.”

exchanges.player: "Another time, perhaps. I had better put the other copies away before dinner. Thank you for taking one." I leave her to her work, put the remaining copies in my room, and go down for the evening meal. I greet the others, sit, and listen while I eat.
exchanges.story:
Caelindra gives the departure a small, formal inclination. “Another time, then.” She turns back to the bridge charters without opening the printed copy.

The remaining stories fit in a neat stack on your desk upstairs. By the evening meal, the dining hall has filled again beneath its lamps and candles. Caelindra arrives with the single copy tucked beneath her notebook and sets both beside her plate. Across the table, Seraphel Dawnquill folds her small white wings close before a server passes with a tureen.

“The soup is warm, the bread is near,” Seraphel says,
“A paper may wait another year.”

Rashid's hand rests on a folded document beside his bowl. “Not another year. I received the instructor's report.”

Ashara looks up from her plate. Aldric does as well.

“The court was not at fault,” Rashid continues. “Practice continued after the instructor left, and the injury happened then. I am revising the request: limited hours, a named supervisor, and no independent sparring.”

“That is a request I can support,” Aldric says.

Ashara tears a piece of bread. “It also leaves my booking intact. Submit it.”

Rashid unfolds the report once more, reading a line before folding it again. “The regular attendees will sign tomorrow.”

Around the table, supper resumes. Seraphel breaks bread into even pieces; Caelindra begins her meal with the story still unopened at her elbow.

exchanges.player: I finish my meal and linger over tea with whoever stays at the table. "Do people ever play music here in the evenings?" I ask the group.
exchanges.story:
As the meal breaks apart, Ashara takes up her training coat and leaves by the garden doors. Aldric excuses himself toward the chapel. Caelindra carries her notebook and the unopened story back toward the library, while Rashid, Ysolde, Thessaly, and Seraphel remain with their tea.

Rashid answers first. “People do, informally. The common room is permitted until ninth bell, if no one is trying to work there.”

“Its acoustics are poor,” Ysolde says. She lifts her cup, considering the steam. “That does not prevent music.”

Thessaly rests both hands around her own tea. “The poor player is usually forgiven. The one who insists on being admired is not.”

Seraphel's blue eyes move toward the firelit doorway of the common room.

“By firelight, later, if you choose,
I have a song that needs no news.”

Rashid gives a small, practical nod. “There are instruments in the common room cabinet. Most of them belong to former residents, so treat them as borrowed.”

Beyond the dining hall, the house's fireplace sends a low amber light across the study tables. The tea remains warm, and the evening has not yet reached the ninth bell.

exchanges.player: "I would like to hear it." I take my tea into the common room and sit near the fire. I do not play an instrument myself; I listen to Seraphel's song if she comes through to sing.
exchanges.story:
Seraphel comes through the doorway after a moment, carrying her tea in one hand. Her small wings settle close against the white-and-gold fabric at her back as she crosses to the cabinet. From it she chooses a narrow-bodied lute, tests two strings, and sits in a leather chair opposite the fire.

Ysolde takes the chair near the window. Thessaly remains by the dining-hall threshold, her cup held between both hands. Rashid stays long enough to lower the lamps nearest the study tables, leaving the fire and the nearer wall lamps to light the room.

Seraphel plucks a quiet opening pattern. Then she sings:

“Bread on the board and boots by the door,
The road may wait for morning's shore;
Keep one lamp against the rain,
And welcome home the lost again.”

The tune is plain and unhurried, carried by the lute more than by force of voice. She repeats it once, changing the last chord into something softer before letting the strings fall still.

For a few moments, only the fire answers. Thessaly sets her cup on a side table. Ysolde looks from the dark window back to Seraphel.

“That is a good song for a house,” Ysolde says.

Seraphel lowers her gaze to the lute and gives its strings one last, gentle touch.

Slate.kind: three held-out continuations of a pilot-authored starting state

exchanges.player: "I am not looking for a verdict on whether he is a good person. Does the situation hold your interest so far?" I let Caelindra read the three pages. Privately, I wonder whether I have made the keeper too obviously resemble Rashid; I do not say that aloud.
exchanges.story:
Caelindra reads in silence, one hand resting lightly over the lower corner of each page as she turns it. At the end, she returns to the first sheet and traces the margin beside the keeper's departure with one pale fingernail.

"Yes," she says at last. "It holds my interest. The keeper has two duties, and neither is trivial. That is sufficient."

She looks across the table, violet eyes level. "The absent replacement is the sharper matter. Medicine can be carried by someone. The light cannot be tended by everyone at once. Whether he had reason to trust that arrangement is more interesting than whether he meant well."

The pages are squared carefully against the tabletop. "Do not arrange a calamity merely to demonstrate that darkness is serious. The dark is already serious to anyone who had expected the lamp."

The library clock gives a thin quarter-bell. Caelindra leaves her own book face-down beside the inkwell and keeps the manuscript between you rather than sliding it back.

exchanges.player: "Thank you. I will think about the replacement." I take the manuscript back and leave her to her book. At lunch I find Rashid. "Are we still set for this afternoon?" I have not told anyone besides Sela about the changed time or location.
exchanges.story:
At lunch, Rashid occupies one end of the long dining table with a page laid beside his bowl. He looks up from it at once.

"We are. Sixth bell at the press." He taps the page with one claw-tipped finger. "I revised the wording after morning practice. Supervised access for the group, a posted inspection of the court, and a review after two weeks. That gives the faculty a way to say yes without pretending no one was hurt."

He folds the sheet along its existing crease, keeping the edges aligned. "If it prints cleanly, I will have the regular group sign it before drills tomorrow."

His attention remains on you, steady and expectant, while the room carries on around the table.

exchanges.player: "The press has a cracked platen. Sela moved my own work to fourth bell in the west workshop. I can read your revised request now, but I will not print it; my booking is for the story. You will need to arrange the request separately." I hold out my hand for the sheet.
exchanges.story:
Rashid looks from your outstretched hand to the folded request. He smooths the sheet open once before placing it across your palm.

"Read it. Your booking is for your story; I had no right to spend it without asking."

He closes his notebook with both hands. "I did take our meeting at the press for an arrangement, though. The change in time and room changes whether people can sign before morning drills. Tell me about changes like that when they happen."

For a moment, the dining hall's clink of cutlery fills the space between you. Rashid draws his untouched cup nearer.

"I will speak with Sela about a separate booking at the hand press. If that does not work, I will make enough copies another way."

established_conversation.content: At dinner I tell Rashid, with Ashara sitting across from us, "I will be at the press tomorrow at sixth bell. You can find me there then."
Rashid puts a small mark beside the appointment in his notebook. "Sixth bell. I can bring the revised request then." Ashara continues eating; neither of them asks about the printing.
Later I go alone to speak to the press steward.

The pressroom is empty except for the steward, Sela. She shows you a crack in the platen. "I cannot run this safely tomorrow. We will have to use the hand press in the west workshop. It is free at fourth bell, if that suits you." The door is shut; the workshop passage outside is quiet.

"Fourth bell in the west workshop is fine. Please leave the change to me; I will tell Rashid myself." I return to my room and keep the change to myself. The next morning I bring three manuscript pages to the library to show Caelindra. My unfinished story concerns a lighthouse keeper who leaves his post to obtain medicine for a sick neighbor. His replacement fails to arrive, and the lighthouse remains dark until midnight. I have not written what happens to any ships or how the story ends.

Caelindra sits at the library window with a book propped against the inkwell. She lays it face-down when you set the pages on the table. "I have a quarter of an hour." She turns the first page. Rashid is elsewhere at morning practice, and nobody else is within earshot.
